stack.title: King David and Bathsheba
stack.hook: David slept with somebody's wife, got her pregnant, and killed her husband. And he still gets called a man after God's own heart.

cards.head: David slept with somebody’s wife, got her pregnant, and killed her husband.
cards.body: And he still gets called a man after God’s own heart. Here’s the story of King David.

cr.artwork: Rembrandt - Bathsheba at Her Bath - WGA19090.jpg
cr.file: Rembrandt - Bathsheba at Her Bath - WGA19090.jpg
cr.line: Rembrandt - Bathsheba at Her Bath - WGA19090.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: The Shepherd Who Became King
cards.body: David started as a shepherd boy. God chose him to become the future king of Israel, even though he was the youngest son in his family and nobody expected him to be chosen.

cr.artwork: Eugène Siberdt - The Prophet Nathan rebukes King David.jpg
cr.file: Eugène Siberdt - The Prophet Nathan rebukes King David.jpg
cr.line: Eugène Siberdt - The Prophet Nathan rebukes King David.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: He became famous after defeating Goliath, eventually became king, and grew into one of the most powerful rulers in Israel’s history.
cards.body: The Bible portrays David as someone who genuinely loved and trusted God.

cr.line: Caravaggio-david-goliath-fin.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: David and Bathsheba
cards.body: Then David did something terrible. One evening, he saw a woman named Bathsheba bathing. She was married to Uriah, one of David’s soldiers. David sent for her and slept with her. Soon afterward, Bathsheba sent David a message: “I am pregnant.” David knew the baby was his.

cr.artwork: Gerard van Honthorst - King David Playing the Harp - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.file: Gerard van Honthorst - King David Playing the Harp - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.line: Gerard van Honthorst - King David Playing the Harp - Google Art Project.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: David Tried to Cover It Up
cards.body: David called Uriah home from the war, hoping Uriah would sleep with Bathsheba so everyone would assume the baby was his. But Uriah refused to enjoy being home while his fellow soldiers were still fighting. So David came up with another plan.

cr.artwork: Beham, Sebald - Scenes from the Life of David - 1534.jpg
cr.file: Beham, Sebald - Scenes from the Life of David - 1534.jpg
cr.line: Beham, Sebald - Scenes from the Life of David - 1534.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: He ordered Uriah to be placed at the front of the fiercest battle, then ordered the other soldiers to pull back.

cr.line: 081.David Mourns the Death of Absalom.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: “You Are the Man”
cards.body: David thought he had gotten away with it. Then God sent the prophet Nathan to him. Nathan told David a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s only beloved lamb. David became furious and demanded that the rich man be punished.

cr.line: Rembrandt - Bathsheba receiving David's Letter.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: Nathan looked at David and said: “You are the man.” David admitted, “I have sinned against the Lord.”

cr.line: David&Bathsheba.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: Forgiveness Did Not Erase the Consequences
cards.body: God forgave David, but that did not erase the consequences of what he had done. The child David and Bathsheba conceived died. David’s family later became consumed by conflict, betrayal, sexual violence, and murder.

cr.artwork: The Toilet of Bathsheba MET DP145915.jpg
cr.file: The Toilet of Bathsheba MET DP145915.jpg
cr.line: The Toilet of Bathsheba MET DP145915.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: His own son Absalom eventually rebelled against him and attempted to take his throne.
cards.body: The Bible does not pretend David’s actions did not matter just because he repented.

cr.line: Verhaeren - Rembrandt, Laurens p081.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: Why Was He Still “A Man After God’s Own Heart”?
cards.body: It was not because David was morally perfect. The phrase first appears before the Bathsheba story. Later, Acts describes David as someone who would carry out God’s purposes.

cr.artwork: Giacomo del Pò - King David Playing the Harp - WGA17985.jpg
cr.file: Giacomo del Pò - King David Playing the Harp - WGA17985.jpg
cr.line: Giacomo del Pò - King David Playing the Harp - WGA17985.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: David failed badly, but when confronted with his sin, he confessed and repented instead of abandoning God.
cards.body: That is one of the central ideas of David’s story: Being after God’s heart does not mean never doing wrong. It means continuing to turn your heart back toward God.

cr.artwork: Hendrick ter Brugghen - King David playing the harp among angels - M.Ob.529 MNW - National Museum in Warsaw.jpg
cr.file: Hendrick ter Brugghen - King David playing the harp among angels - M.Ob.529 MNW - National Museum in Warsaw.jpg
cr.line: Hendrick ter Brugghen - King David playing the harp among angels - M.Ob.529 MNW - National Museum in Warsaw.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY DAVID IS STILL THE TEST CASE
cards.body: Most traditions quietly drop their heroes' worst behaviour. This one keeps it in the text. That refusal is why the story is still argued about rather than settled.
